Where a digital elevation model comes from, what it costs to fetch, what happens
when you put a graph *on* a surface rather than *above* it, and what a slope is
worth once it is an edge attribute. The eight notebooks before this one draw on
a plane, which claims every edge costs the same to walk in either direction.

The site is the Albaicín in Granada rather than the Ciutat Vella of the rest of
the suite, for a measured reason: central València has 21 m of relief across the
1.2 km frame, under 2 % of its width. Two of the figures are of failures, kept
because neither raises: a network that sinks into the hillside after being
sampled at one resolution while the surface was built at another, and a finer
mesh that buys a smoother surface and not one meter of extra relief, because the
source is 30 m data either way.

Nothing here needs an API key. The keyed route (OpenTopography) and the file
route (a GeoTIFF you already have) are switched off at the top, since both need
`rasterio`, which Blender's Python does not ship.

For the same operations from the sidebar, see the
[Elevation panel](../panels/osmnx/elevation.qmd) and its
[tutorial](../tutorials/panels/osmnx/elevation.qmd), and
[Tutorial 3](../examples/03-urban-terrain.qmd).
